items.question_en: Consider a small block sliding down an inclined plane of inclination 30° with the horizontal. The coefficient of friction is μ = ⅔x, where x is the distance (in meter) through which the mass slides down. The distance covered by the mass before it stops is

solution.approach: The block starts and ends at rest, so the work done by gravity along the slope must equal the work done against a friction force that grows with distance.

steps.text: Write the friction force at a distance x down the slope, using the given coefficient.
Set the work done by gravity over the whole distance d equal to the work done against friction, since the block starts and ends at rest.
steps.why_this_step: The net work on the block is zero because its kinetic energy is zero both before it starts and after it stops.

steps.text: Evaluate the integral and cancel mg from both sides.
Solve for d.

common_mistakes.text: Using the friction coefficient at the final position, μ(d), as if it were constant along the whole slide, instead of integrating the growing friction force, gives d = √3/2 m.
Leaving out cos30° from the normal force in the friction term gives a different, unlisted distance of 1.5 m.

items.question_en: Ball P of mass m moving with velocity 'v' collides with another ball Q of mass 2m, at rest. If v_P and v_Q are the final velocities of P and Q respectively, after collision, then: (Assume the coefficient of restitution is 1/3)

solution.approach: Momentum conservation and the restitution equation together fix both final velocities, giving the ratio that is asked for.

steps.text: Write momentum conservation for the two balls.
Write the restitution equation using the given coefficient.
steps.why_this_step: The coefficient of restitution compares the separation speed after impact to the approach speed before impact.

steps.text: Solve the two equations together for the final velocities.
Divide to get the ratio asked for.

common_mistakes.text: Writing the ratio the other way round, v_P/v_Q instead of v_Q/v_P, attaches the 4 to the wrong ball.
Assuming the collision is perfectly elastic instead of using the given coefficient of restitution 1/3 gives v_Q/v_P = 2.

items.question_en: A moving particle collides with a stationary particle of mass 1/n times the mass of moving particle, the fraction of its kinetic energy transferred to the stationary particle is

solution.approach: For a head-on elastic collision, the fraction of kinetic energy handed to the struck particle follows a standard formula in the mass ratio.

steps.text: Write the fraction of kinetic energy transferred to a stationary target in an elastic collision.
steps.why_this_step: This comes from solving momentum conservation and kinetic energy conservation together for an elastic collision.

steps.text: Substitute the given masses, the moving particle m₁ = m and the stationary one m₂ = m/n.
Simplify by cancelling m² and clearing the fraction inside the bracket.

common_mistakes.text: Squaring the velocity-transfer ratio 2m₁/(m₁+m₂) directly and calling it the energy fraction, without weighting it by the mass ratio, gives 4n²/(1+n)².
Expanding (m₁+m₂)² as m₁²+m₂², dropping the cross term, gives 4n/(1+n²).
Dropping the denominator (1+n)² after finding the numerator 4n² leaves only 4n².

items.question_en: The potential energy of an object is U(x) = (5x² − 4x³) J, where x is the position in meter. The position at which the force becomes zero is

solution.approach: The force is the negative slope of the potential energy, so setting it to zero and solving for the nonzero position gives the answer.

steps.text: Differentiate U(x) with respect to x.
Write the force and set it to zero.
Factor and solve, keeping the nonzero root.

common_mistakes.text: Taking x = 0, the trivial root where the object has not moved at all, instead of the nonzero position asked for.

items.question_en: A body of mass 'm' slides down along a frictionless inclined plane from height 'h' and just completes motion in a vertical circle of radius 2m after reaching the bottom. What is the value of h? [Use g = 10 m/s²]

solution.approach: Energy conservation from the top of the incline to the top of the loop, combined with the minimum-speed condition at the top of the loop, gives the height.

steps.text: Write the minimum speed condition at the top of the loop, where gravity alone supplies the centripetal force.
Apply energy conservation from the release height h to the top of the loop, which is at height 2R above the bottom.
Substitute v_top² = gR and solve for h.

common_mistakes.text: Thinking the release height only needs to equal the radius R, missing the extra R/2 that comes from the required speed at the top, gives 2 m instead of 5 m.

items.question_en: The displacement 's' of a body of mass 3 kg under the action of a force is given by s = t³/3, where 's' is in metres and 't' is in seconds. The work done by the force in the first two seconds is

solution.approach: The given force is the only one doing work, so the work it does equals the change in kinetic energy.

steps.text: Differentiate the displacement to get the velocity.
Evaluate the velocity at the start and at the end of the two seconds.
Apply the work-energy theorem over this interval.
steps.why_this_step: The work-energy theorem holds for the net force, and here the given force is the only one doing work.

common_mistakes.text: Multiplying the force at t = 2 s by the total displacement, instead of using the work-energy theorem, gives 12 N × 8/3 m = 32 J.
Leaving out the one-half in the kinetic energy formula gives 3 × 4² = 48 J.

items.question_en: A body of mass 3 kg is moving under the action of a force which causes a displacement of (t³/3) m, where 't' is time in seconds. The work done by the force in first 2 seconds is

solution.approach: The given force is the only one doing work, so the work it does equals the change in kinetic energy over the two seconds.

steps.text: Differentiate the displacement to get the velocity.
Evaluate the velocity at the start and at the end of the two seconds.
Apply the work-energy theorem over this interval.
steps.why_this_step: The work-energy theorem holds for the net force, and here the given force is the only one doing work.

common_mistakes.text: Leaving out the one-half in the kinetic energy formula gives 3 × 4² = 48 J instead of 24 J.

items.question_en: A body falls freely from a height 'h' on a fixed horizontal plane and rebounds. If 'e' is the coefficient of restitution, the total distance travelled before it comes to rest is

solution.approach: Each bounce rises to a height reduced by e² from the previous one, and the total path length is the sum of this geometric series of up-and-down trips.

steps.text: Write the rebound height after the first bounce in terms of the coefficient of restitution.
steps.why_this_step: The rebound speed is e times the impact speed, and height is proportional to the square of the speed.

steps.text: Write the total distance as the initial fall plus twice every rebound height, since each rebound is climbed and then fallen again.
Sum the infinite geometric series with first term e²h and common ratio e².
Combine into a single fraction.

common_mistakes.text: Counting only the rise of each bounce and not also the fall back down, missing the factor of 2 for each rebound, gives total = h/(1−e²), which is not among the printed options.

items.question_en: The sphere A of mass m moving with a constant velocity hits another sphere B of mass 2m at rest. If the coefficient of restitution is 0.4, the ratio of the velocities of the spheres A and B after collision is

solution.approach: Momentum conservation and the restitution equation together fix both spheres' final velocities, whose ratio is the answer.

steps.text: Write momentum conservation for the two spheres.
Write the restitution equation using e = 0.4.
Solve the two equations together.
Form the ratio asked for.

common_mistakes.text: Writing the restitution equation with the velocities swapped, v_A′ − v_B′ = e·v instead of v_B′ − v_A′ = e·v, gives v_A:v_B = 3:1.
Assuming the collision is perfectly elastic (e = 1) instead of using the given e = 0.4 gives a ratio of 1:2, which is not among the printed options.

items.question_en: The kinetic energy of a body of mass 4 kg moving with a velocity of (2î − 4ĵ − k̂) ms⁻¹ is

solution.approach: Kinetic energy depends on the square of the speed, found by squaring and adding the components of the velocity vector.

steps.text: Find the square of the speed from the components.
Apply the kinetic energy formula.

common_mistakes.text: Leaving out the one-half in the kinetic energy formula gives 4 × 21 = 84 J.
Using a mass of 6 kg by mistake instead of the given 4 kg gives ½ × 6 × 21 = 63 J.
Reporting the speed-squared value itself, 21, as the kinetic energy, without multiplying by ½m, gives 21 J.

items.question_en: A ball P of mass 0.5 kg moving with a velocity of 10 ms⁻¹ collides with another ball Q of mass 1 kg at rest. If the coefficient of restitution is 0.4, the ratio of the velocities of the balls P and Q after the collision is

solution.approach: Momentum conservation and the restitution equation together fix both balls' final velocities, whose ratio is the answer.

steps.text: Write momentum conservation for the two balls.
Write the restitution equation using e = 0.4.
Solve the two equations together.
steps.equation: v_P = 2/3 m s⁻¹,  v_Q = 14/3 m s⁻¹

steps.text: Form the ratio asked for.

common_mistakes.text: Mistaking the coefficient of restitution itself for the ratio of the final velocities gives 0.4 = 2/5, so v_P:v_Q = 2:5.
Reducing the ratio 2:14 by dividing only the second number by 2, and leaving the first as it is, gives 2:7 instead of 1:7.

items.question_en: The work done in displacing a particle from y = a to y = 2a by a force −K/y² acting along y-axis is

solution.approach: The work done by a position-dependent force is the definite integral of the force over the displacement.

steps.text: Write the work as the integral of the force from y = a to y = 2a.
steps.equation: W = ∫ (−K/y²) dy, taken from y = a to y = 2a

steps.text: Integrate.
steps.equation: W = K/y, evaluated from y = a to y = 2a = K/(2a) − K/a

steps.text: Simplify.

common_mistakes.text: Using the average of the force at the two endpoints, y = a and y = 2a, times the displacement a, instead of integrating, gives −5K/8a.
Evaluating the force only at the starting point y = a and reporting it directly as the work, instead of integrating over the displacement, gives −K/a².

items.question_en: A body of mass 0.5 kg is supplied with a power 'P' (in watt) which varies with time 't' (in second) as P = 3t² + 3. If the velocity of the body at time t = 0 is zero, then the velocity of the body at time t = 3s is

solution.approach: Power is the rate of doing work, so integrating it over time gives the kinetic energy gained, from which the final speed follows.

steps.text: Write power as the time derivative of kinetic energy.
Integrate the power over the three seconds to get the total work done.
Set this equal to the gain in kinetic energy and solve for the speed at t = 3 s.

common_mistakes.text: Taking the numerical value of the work done, 36, directly as the final speed instead of solving ½mv² = 36 for v, gives 36 m s⁻¹.
Using the power at t = 3 s alone, P(3) = 30 W, as if it equalled the final kinetic energy, instead of integrating power over the three seconds, gives a different, wrong speed.

items.question_en: If the kinetic energy of a body moving with a velocity of (2î + 3ĵ − 4k̂) ms⁻¹ is 87 J, then the mass of the body is

solution.approach: Kinetic energy depends on the square of the speed, found by squaring and adding the components of the velocity vector.

steps.text: Find the square of the speed from the vector components.
Apply the kinetic energy formula and solve for the mass.

common_mistakes.text: Leaving out the one-half in the kinetic energy formula, dividing 87 directly by v² = 29, gives a mass of 3 kg.
Using ¼mv² instead of ½mv² for the kinetic energy formula gives 87/(0.25×29), a mass of 12 kg.
Adding the velocity components before squaring, (2+3−4)² = 1, instead of squaring each component first, gives a badly wrong speed.
